reading.title: In the garden
reading.text:
On Sunday my grandfather works in the garden. He wears an old hat and he takes me with him.

He grows carrots, potatoes, and a lot of tomatoes. I pick the tomatoes because they are easy to find. He talks to the plants while he works.

We come inside late. My hands are dirty and my grandfather is happy. We eat the tomatoes before dinner, all of them.

reading.title: How to tell if a vegetable is fresh
reading.text:
Children learn quickly that a carrot should be firm and a lettuce leaf should be crisp, long before anyone explains why. What takes longer to understand is that freshness is not something you can see from across a shop. A vegetable can look perfect and still be several days old.

This is why weight is often a better guide than colour. A fresh carrot feels heavy for its size, and it snaps rather than bends. A wilted lettuce feels light in the hand and its leaves fold instead of breaking.

Smell helps too. Fresh vegetables smell faintly of the earth or of nothing at all. A strong smell, especially a sour one, usually means it is time to throw them away.

options: That a carrot should be firm

questions.q: What is often a better guide than colour?

reading.title: The organic question
reading.text:
An organic carrot and a conventional carrot are, to most eyes, indistinguishable, and this is precisely what makes the label so difficult to think about clearly. The difference is not in what the vegetable looks like on the plate, but in what happened to the soil, the water and the workers long before it arrived there. Buying organic is, in large part, a bet on a process you cannot see.

This does not mean the bet is a foolish one. Vegetables grown without synthetic pesticides tend to support more insect life in the surrounding soil, and farms that avoid heavy fertiliser use tend to leave the land in better condition for the next season. Neither of those facts, however, guarantees that the carrot itself is more nutritious, and studies on that particular question have mostly found the difference to be small.

What is worth noticing is that the honest reasons to choose organic are mostly about the field, not the food. That is not a weaker reason than taste or nutrition. It is simply a different one, and it is worth choosing for the right reason rather than the reason on the packaging.

questions.q: What does the writer say is hard to see when buying organic?
What does the writer say about nutrition studies?
options: They mostly found a small difference
They found organic is always better
They found no vegetables are nutritious
